panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal post-contrast MRI clearly showing enhancement of the roof of the middle ear cavity and adjacent cerebelli, which is highly specific for petrous apicitis/Gradenigo syndrome. B: Coronal post-contrast MRI demonstrating superomedial extension of the infection to involve the floor of the middle cranial fossa and the cavernous sinus, which are known extensions of petrous apicitis.

in_text_mentions: ging (MRI; Figure 2B). Subtle evidence of petrous apicitis of his right temporal bone was demonstrated by MRI (Figure 2C). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: The T1-weighted MRI shows hypointense signal on the right petrous apex compared to the contralateral side, consistent with petrous apicitis. B: Enhanced T1-weighted MRI demonstrates prominent enhancement of the right petrous apex and mild dural enhancement, highly suggestive of petrous apicitis. C: The T2-weighted MRI shows hyperintense signal in the right petrous apex compared to the contralateral side, indicating inflammation or edema consistent with petrous apicitis.

plate_findings.evidence: continued osseous erosion of the right petrous temporal bone

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The panel shows an axial CT of a patient with a case of Gradenigo's Syndrome. It demonstrates osseous erosion of the right petrous temporal bone, which is a key manifestation of the disease. The context confirms this is a repeat CT showing worsening disease progression. B: The panel shows a coronal CT of a patient with a case of Gradenigo's Syndrome. It demonstrates continued and spreading osseous erosion (indicated by red arrows) to the clivus and right occipital condyle, showing disease progression as described in the caption and text.

plate_findings.evidence: bilateral middle ear and mastoid effusions with extension to the petrous apex with septal enhancement.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows MR imagery (MRV) of the head demonstrating bilateral middle ear and mastoid effusions, petrous apex enhancement, and an adjacent collection, consistent with petrous apicitis and associated inflammatory changes in the skull base, matching the diagnosis of Gradenigo syndrome. B: Panel B displays MR vascular imaging of the internal carotid artery showing enhancement and moderate luminal narrowing of the right ICA, which is mentioned in the text as being associated with the presentation of the disease.
panels.attribution_text: Tao et al. Ceftazidime-Cefazolin Empiric Therapy for Pediatric Gradenigo Syndrome.. The Annals of otology, rhinology, and laryngology 2025. doi:10.1177/00034894241301289. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MRV head on admission. Paranasal sinus disease without invasive changes. There are bilateral middle ear and mastoid effusions with extension to the petrous apex with septal enhancement. At the rigth petrous apex and clivus, there is enhancement, patchy edema, loss of normal fine septations, and smooth osseous margins. A 5.9 mm extra-axial collection was appreciated on the right side of the prepontine cistern overlying the petroclival synchondrosis, which with associated diffusion restriction, was in keeping with a small abscess. There was asymmetric increased T2 FLAIR and postcontrast enhancement involving the wall of the petrosal and proximal cavernous segments of the right internal carotid arter with moderate luminal narrowing within these segments. No cerebral venonus sinus thrombosis was appreciated.
in_text_mentions: Magnetic resonance venography (MRV; Figure 1) on admission demonstrated otomastoiditis with coalescent right petrous apicitis, clival osteomyelitis and a 5.9 mm adjacent extradural abscess overlying the right petroclival synchondrosis. Paranasal sinus disease was noted without invasive changes. Finally, there was asymmetric enhancement involving the right carotid canal with moderate narrowing of the right internal carotid artery (ICA). No cerebral venous sinus thrombosis was evident.

plate_findings.evidence: CT demonstrates bony lucency within this area potentially suggestive of a small Brodie's abscess.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is an MRI showing interval improvement of inflammatory changes associated with the diagnosis of Gradenigo Syndrome (petrous apicitis). B: Panel B is a CT scan demonstrating resolution of mass effect on the right Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) and improved otomastoid opacification related to the petrous apicitis. C: Panel C is a CT scan showing bony lucency suggestive of Brodie's abscess formation, a finding associated with the chronic/resolving petrous apicitis.
panels.attribution_text: Tao et al. Ceftazidime-Cefazolin Empiric Therapy for Pediatric Gradenigo Syndrome.. The Annals of otology, rhinology, and laryngology 2025. doi:10.1177/00034894241301289. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (A) MRI at follow-up week 1. There is interval improvement of the inflammatory changes involving the right petrosal-clival junction, sphenoid sinus, and right petrous apex. The small focus of diffusion restriction at the right lateral clivus, noted at admission, is no longer present. (B) There is interval improvement of the right ICA caliber likely from resolving surrounding inflammation and associated mass effect. Improved otomastoid opacification noted with some residual fluid especially at the right petrous apex. (C) CT demonstrates bony lucency within this area potentially suggestive of a small Brodie's abscess.
in_text_mentions: After 3 days, the patient’s diplopia and ocular dysmotility had resolved. Repeat neuroimaging (Figure 2) at one-week post-admission showed improved ICA caliber and osteomyelitis, but with interval development of a small Brodie’s abscess, which prompted 1 additional week of intravenous antibiotic treatment (2 weeks total). Subsequently, he completed a 4-week course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and ciprofloxacin. panels.rationale: This MRV image of a child demonstrates pathology in the right petrous apex region consistent with purulent contents and enhancement (petrous apicitis) as described in the caption and text, correlating with the primary disease key. The image also shows venous sinus thrombosis as a complication, linking the findings clearly.

panels.figure_caption: MRV on admission demonstrating thrombus in the right sigmoid and distal transverse sinuses extending to the proximal internal jugular vein; a presumed infected thrombus.
in_text_mentions: An MRI of the brain with and without contrast was obtained (Figure 2), which revealed right mastoid enhancement and notable coalescent purulent contents within the petrous apex, concerning for right mastoiditis and right petrous apicitis. A thrombosis was discovered involving the right sigmoid and distal transverse sinuses, extending to the proximal portion of the internal jugular vein, visualized on MRV (Figure 3). The patient was immediately transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for elevated care.
